previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with relapsed multiple myeloma, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, type 2 diabetes, chronic diastolic heart failure, and CKD stage 3, was admitted for recurrent syncope occurring while seated during a blood pressure check. The episode was consistent with neurocardiogenic syncope, similar to a recent prior event. His low heart rate on carvedilol was thought to contribute, so the dose was reduced from 12.5 mg BID to 6.25 mg BID and amlodipine increased to 10 mg daily to maintain blood pressure control. He remained stable without further syncopal episodes, was evaluated by cardiology, and discharged with a Zio patch for outpatient heart monitoring. His anemia remained stable on prednisone, folic acid, and B12, with a single unit of packed red blood cells given near discharge due to low hemoglobin. His CKD, diabetes, and cytopenias were managed without acute intervention. He was discharged home with services, under 24-hour supervision, and with follow-up planned in oncology, cardiology, and primary care.

diarrhea and ___ edema/erythema. Patient was treated within last 
couple months for episode of bilateral ___ cellulitis. Over the

bilateral shins but no warmth, drainage, or obvious fluctuance.

leukocytosis on labs drawn in clinic. His symptoms were thought

brewing cellulitis. Consulted dermatology who thought his

no further episodes of diarrhea during the admission. He also 
had one episode of symptomatic hypoglycemia to 56. He was given 
juice and improved quickly. He had his Lantus decreased to 25 
units QAM and will be discharged on this lower dose. He was 
hemodynamically stable at the time of discharge and will follow 
up with Dr. ___ in ___ ___ clinic and with ___ 
Cardiology.

Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you. You were admitted because 
you were having diarrhea and increased swelling and redness in 
your legs. Your diarrhea resolved on its own, and your legs were 
evaluated by dermatology. They believe that your current 
symptoms are not due to an infection but to venous stasis 
changes, which occur when there is poor blood return from your 
legs which causes pooling in your extremities. They recommended 
that you keep your legs elevated and wrap them snugly in ACE 
bandages.

When you are discharged, it is important to take your 
medications as directed. We decreased your morning Lantus 
because you had one episode of low blood sugar while in the 
hospital. You will now take 25 units every morning. Otherwise, 
your medications will be kept the same, and you will follow up
